--- title: "Point Pattern Analysis, Predictive Checks, and Spatial Econometrics of Madrid AirBnb Prices" description: "Spatial point pattern analysis, IDW price interpolation, and spatial econometric modelling of Madrid Airbnb listing prices." date: "2024-03-21" image: sem_air.svg categories: [R, Spatial Econometrics, Spatial Analysis, Airbnb] bibliography: references.bib csl: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/citation-style-language/styles/master/ieee.csl --- ## Introduction & Setup This report investigates the spatial distribution and determinants of AirBnb property prices in Madrid, Spain, addressing the research tasks set out at the end of **Chapter 4** (*Point Data Analysis*), **Chapter 5** (*Spatial Interaction & Predictive Checking*), and **Chapter 6** (*Spatial Econometrics*). ### Required Libraries We begin by loading the required spatial analysis, interpolation, econometric, and visualisation libraries in R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Data manipulation and transformation library(tidyverse) library(stringr) # Spatial data handling and interpolation library(sf) library(sp) library(gstat) library(hexbin) # Spatial weights and spatial econometrics library(spdep) library(spatialreg) # Simulation and model diagnostics library(arm) # Visualisation, mapping, and tables library(ggplot2) library(gridExtra) library(tmap) library(viridis) library(RColorBrewer) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) # Disable spherical geometry (s2) for planar grid/interpolation compatibility sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE) set.seed(453) ``` ::: ### Madrid AirBnb Dataset We load the pre-processed Madrid AirBnb GeoPackage (`madrid_abb.gpkg`) from `data/data_r/se_m_airbnb/assignment_1_madrid/` [@lovelace2019; @bivand2013]. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Robust relative path detection across development environments data_candidates <- c( file.path("..", "..", "..", "data", "data_r", "se_m_airbnb", "assignment_1_madrid", "madrid_abb.gpkg"), file.path("data", "data_r", "se_m_airbnb", "assignment_1_madrid", "madrid_abb.gpkg"), "/Users/jay/Desktop/websiteV02/data/data_r/se_m_airbnb/assignment_1_madrid/madrid_abb.gpkg" ) data_path <- data_candidates[file.exists(data_candidates)][1] mad_abb <- st_read(data_path, quiet = TRUE) ``` ::: Let us inspect the available attributes, coordinate reference system (CRS), and summary statistics of the dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} colnames(mad_abb) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "price" "price_usd" "log1p_price_usd" "accommodates" [5] "bathrooms_text" "bathrooms" "bedrooms" "beds" [9] "neighbourhood" "room_type" "property_type" "WiFi" [13] "Coffee" "Gym" "Parking" "km_to_retiro" [17] "geom" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} st_crs(mad_abb)$input ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "WGS 84" ``` ::: ::: The dataset contains **18399** AirBnb listings across **127** neighbourhoods in Madrid, stored as point geometries in WGS 84 (`EPSG:4326`). Key variables used across this assignment include: - `price_usd`: Nightly listing price in USD ($P_i$). - `log1p_price_usd`: Log-transformed nightly price, $\log(1 + P_i)$. - `accommodates`: Guest capacity of the property ($Acc_i$). - `bathrooms`: Number of bathrooms ($Bath_i$). - `bedrooms`: Number of bedrooms ($Bedr_i$). - `beds`: Number of beds ($Beds_i$). - `neighbourhood`: Neighbourhood name ($r$) within Madrid. - `km_to_retiro`: Euclidean distance (km) from the property to El Retiro Park. - `WiFi`, `Coffee`, `Gym`, `Parking`: Binary amenity indicators (`1` = present, `0` = absent). - `geom`: Point geometry ($X$ longitude, $Y$ latitude). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} desc_stats <- mad_abb %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::select(price_usd, log1p_price_usd, accommodates, bathrooms, bedrooms, beds, km_to_retiro) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% group_by(Variable) %>% summarise( N = n(), Mean = round(mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), SD = round(sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), Min = round(min(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), Median = round(median(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), IQR = round(IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), Max = round(max(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 2), .groups = "drop" ) kable( desc_stats, caption = "Table 1.1: Descriptive Statistics of Key Madrid AirBnb Variables" ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: --- ## Point Data Analysis (Chapter 4 Tasks) Chapter 4 focuses on visualising dense spatial point patterns and interpolating continuous attribute surfaces from point samples [@comber2015]. ### Exploratory Price Distribution & Spatial Binning Before constructing the spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) surfaces, we examine the non-spatial distribution of raw (`price_usd`) versus log-transformed (`log1p_price_usd`) prices, alongside 2D spatial binning of listing coordinates. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Histogram + 1D KDE of raw price_usd p_raw_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = price_usd)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") + geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) + labs( title = "Raw AirBnb Price (USD)", x = "Price (USD)", y = "Density" ) + theme_minimal() # Histogram + 1D KDE of log1p_price_usd p_log_hist <- ggplot(mad_abb, aes(x = log1p_price_usd)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, aes(y = after_stat(density)), fill = "grey35", colour = "white") + geom_density(fill = "#FF6666", alpha = 0.45, colour = "#FF6666", linewidth = 0.8) + labs( title = "Log-Transformed AirBnb Price", x = "log(1 + Price USD)", y = "Density" ) + theme_minimal() grid.arrange(p_raw_hist, p_log_hist, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.1: Distribution and 1D KDE of Raw USD Prices (left) vs. Log-Transformed Prices (right) in Madrid.](index_files/figure-html/fig_nonspatial_kde-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Raw AirBnb prices are heavily right-skewed (mean = \$118.98, median = \$60, maximum = \$9999), with most properties clustered below \$150 per night and a thin tail of luxury listings. Taking the natural logarithm (`log1p_price_usd`) compresses extreme values and yields a near-symmetric, bell-shaped distribution centered around 4.19. To address point overplotting across the 18399 locations, we first compare raw point plotting with two-dimensional square binning (`geom_bin2d`) and hexagonal binning (`geom_hex`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mad_coords <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(mad_abb)) # Square 2D binning sqbin <- ggplot() + geom_bin2d(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "Count") + labs(title = "2D Square Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") + coord_equal() + theme_minimal() # Hexagonal 2D binning hexbin_plot <- ggplot() + geom_hex(data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), bins = 40) + scale_fill_continuous(type = "viridis", name = "Count") + labs(title = "2D Hexagonal Binning", x = "Longitude (X)", y = "Latitude (Y)") + coord_equal() + theme_minimal() grid.arrange(sqbin, hexbin_plot, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.2: Spatial Distribution of Madrid AirBnb Listings using Square Binning (left) and Hexagonal Binning (right).](index_files/figure-html/fig_binning-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: ### Task 4.1: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid To obtain a smooth, continuous surface representing the spatial intensity (probability density) of AirBnb property locations across Madrid, we apply two-dimensional Kernel Density Estimation (`stat_density2d_filled`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kde_surface <- ggplot(data = mad_abb) + stat_density2d_filled( data = mad_coords, aes(x = X, y = Y), alpha = 0.85, n = 100 ) + scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "viridis", name = "Density Level") + geom_sf(alpha = 0) + labs( title = "Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Locations in Madrid", subtitle = "Continuous probability surface of listing concentration (WGS 84)", x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude" ) + theme_bw() kde_surface ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.3: Two-Dimensional Spatial Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) of AirBnb Property Locations in Madrid.](index_files/figure-html/fig_spatial_kde-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: **Interpretation of the KDE Surface:** The spatial KDE reveals an intense, monocentric concentration of AirBnb properties in the historic and tourist core of Madrid (`Centro` district, around longitudes $-3.71^\circ$ to $-3.69^\circ$ and latitudes $40.41^\circ$ to $40.43^\circ$, covering neighbourhoods such as *Sol*, *Embajadores*, *Palacio*, *Cortes*, *Justicia*, and *Universidad*). Density decays radially outward into surrounding residential districts (*Chamberí*, *Salamanca*, *Arganzuela*, *Retiro*, and *Tetuán*), with peripheral suburban districts exhibiting very sparse listing density. ### Task 4.2: Spatial Interpolation of AirBnb Prices via Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) While KDE estimates the density of *point occurrences*, it does not show how property *values* vary across space. To construct a continuous surface of AirBnb prices ($\hat{z}(x) = \sum_i w_i z_i / \sum_i w_i$), we apply Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) interpolation [@comber2015; @cressie2015statistics]: 1. **Create a regular target grid (`mad.grid`)**: A $100 \times 100$ grid (10,000 evenly spaced prediction centres) spanning the bounding box of `mad_abb`. 2. **Compute IDW predictions**: Use `gstat::idw()` with `nmax = 150` nearest neighbours for both raw USD prices (`price_usd ~ 1`) and log-transformed prices (`log1p_price_usd ~ 1`). 3. **Render the interpolated raster surfaces**: Map the predicted values (`var1.pred`) across the grid. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. Create a 100 x 100 regular grid of cell centres over Madrid mad.grid <- mad_abb %>% st_bbox() %>% st_as_sfc() %>% st_make_grid( n = 100, what = "centers" ) %>% st_as_sf() %>% cbind(., st_coordinates(.)) # Ensure identical CRS between source locations and target grid st_crs(mad.grid) <- st_crs(mad_abb) # 2. Fit IDW for raw price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours) idw.raw <- idw( price_usd ~ 1, locations = mad_abb, newdata = mad.grid, nmax = 150 ) %>% cbind(st_coordinates(.)) # 3. Fit IDW for log1p_price_usd (nmax = 150 nearest neighbours) idw.log <- idw( log1p_price_usd ~ 1, locations = mad_abb, newdata = mad.grid, nmax = 150 ) %>% cbind(st_coordinates(.)) ``` ::: Let us inspect the first rows of the interpolated IDW spatial object and plot both the raw price surface and the log-price surface. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} head(st_drop_geometry(idw.raw), 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_idw_raw <- ggplot(idw.raw, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) + geom_raster() + scale_fill_viridis_b(option = "viridis", name = "Pred. USD ($)") + theme_void() + geom_sf(alpha = 0) + labs( title = "IDW Surface: Raw Price (USD)", subtitle = "Binned Viridis scale (nmax = 150)" ) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) p_idw_log <- ggplot(idw.log, aes(x = X, y = Y, fill = var1.pred)) + geom_raster() + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Pred. log(Price)") + theme_void() + geom_sf(alpha = 0) + labs( title = "IDW Surface: Log Price", subtitle = "Continuous Magma scale (nmax = 150)" ) + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5)) grid.arrange(p_idw_raw, p_idw_log, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 1.4: Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) Interpolated Surfaces of Madrid AirBnb Prices: Raw USD Price (left) and Log Price (right), using nmax = 150.](index_files/figure-html/fig_idw_surface-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: We can also use the IDW model to predict the nightly price of a single hypothetical property located near El Retiro Park (`X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pt_retiro <- c(X = -3.6830, Y = 40.4153) %>% st_point() %>% st_sfc(crs = st_crs(mad_abb)) %>% st_sf() idw.one <- idw(price_usd ~ 1, locations = mad_abb, newdata = pt_retiro, nmax = 150) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $", round(idw.one$var1.pred[1], 2), "USD\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Predicted nightly price near El Retiro Park: $ 166.67 USD ``` ::: ::: **Interpretation of the IDW Price Surface:** Unlike the KDE map—where intensity peaks strictly in the historic center—the IDW price surface highlights distinct high-price corridors extending into affluent districts such as *Salamanca*, *Chamberí*, *Chamartín* (north-central Madrid), and the eastern perimeter near *San Blas-Canillejas* (around the Wanda Metropolitano stadium and IFEMA exhibition centre), while southern districts (*Usera*, *Villaverde*, *Puente de Vallecas*, *Carabanchel*) form a persistent low-price belt. --- ## Regression Modelling & Predictive Checks (Chapter 5 Tasks) Chapter 5 focuses on building regression models of property prices and evaluating their adequacy through **Predictive Performance Checks (PPC)** that account for both point predictions and inferential/predictive simulation uncertainty [@gelman2006data]. ### Task 5.1: Baseline Linear Regression Model for Raw Price ($P_i$) We first estimate the baseline Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model explaining raw price in USD (`price_usd`) as a linear function of four core structural property characteristics: $$ P_i = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ba.price <- lm(price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb) summary(ba.price) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -694.2 -64.0 -45.4 -20.9 9913.0 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 19.084 6.594 2.894 0.0038 ** accommodates 19.530 2.145 9.106 < 2e-16 *** bathrooms 1.942 4.564 0.426 0.6704 bedrooms 31.953 4.657 6.862 7.02e-12 *** beds -6.064 2.679 -2.264 0.0236 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 358.9 on 18394 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.02277, Adjusted R-squared: 0.02255 F-statistic: 107.1 on 4 and 18394 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ### Task 5.2: Parallel Linear Regression Model for Log Price ($\log(P_i)$) Next, we estimate a parallel OLS specification using the log-transformed price (`log1p_price_usd`) as the dependent variable: $$ \log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ba.log_price <- lm(log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb) summary(ba.log_price) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -3.8386 -0.4740 -0.1069 0.3130 5.4065 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 3.478207 0.014270 243.751 < 2e-16 *** accommodates 0.219752 0.004641 47.348 < 2e-16 *** bathrooms -0.044322 0.009876 -4.488 7.24e-06 *** bedrooms 0.122788 0.010077 12.184 < 2e-16 *** beds -0.060647 0.005797 -10.462 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.7767 on 18394 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.244, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2438 F-statistic: 1484 on 4 and 18394 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: Let us compare the parameter estimates and fit statistics of both models in a formatted table. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ch5_comp <- tibble( Term = c("(Intercept)", "accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds", "R-squared", "Adj. R-squared", "Residual SE"), `Model 1: Raw Price (USD)` = c( sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[1], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[1, 2]), sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[2], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[2, 2]), sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[3], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[3, 2]), sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[4], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[4, 2]), sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)***", coef(ba.price)[5], summary(ba.price)$coefficients[5, 2]), sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.price)$r.squared), sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.price)$adj.r.squared), sprintf("%.2f", summary(ba.price)$sigma) ), `Model 2: Log Price` = c( sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[1], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[1, 2]), sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[2], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[2, 2]), sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[3], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[3, 2]), sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[4], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[4, 2]), sprintf("%.4f (%.4f)***", coef(ba.log_price)[5], summary(ba.log_price)$coefficients[5, 2]), sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.log_price)$r.squared), sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.log_price)$adj.r.squared), sprintf("%.4f", summary(ba.log_price)$sigma) ) ) kable( ch5_comp, caption = "Table 2.1: Comparison of Baseline OLS Models for Raw Price (USD) vs. Log-Transformed Price (Standard Errors in Parentheses; *** p < 0.001)" ) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

accommodates 19.530 (2.145)*** 0.2198 (0.0046)***

bedrooms 31.953 (4.657)*** 0.1228 (0.0101)***

````` ::: ::: ### Task 5.3: Predictive Check Analysis & Model Comparison To evaluate how well each model captures the true data-generating process, we perform two levels of **Predictive Performance Checks (PPC)** following @gelman2006data: 1. **Point-Estimate Predictive Check**: Comparing the empirical kernel density of the deterministic fitted values ($\hat{y}_i = X_i\hat{\beta}$) against the observed outcome distribution ($y_i$). 2. **Simulated Predictive Check (Inferential + Predictive Uncertainty)**: Using `arm::sim()` to draw posterior parameter realisations ($\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}$) and simulating 250 synthetic outcome vectors $\tilde{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(X\tilde{\beta}, \tilde{\sigma}^2)$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1)) # 1. Point-estimate check for Raw Price model plot( density(ba.price$fitted.values), xlim = c(-50, 600), ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$price_usd)$y)) * 1.05), col = "black", lwd = 2, xlab = "Price (USD)", ylab = "Density", main = "Point Check: Raw Price Model" ) lines(density(mad_abb$price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2) legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n") # 2. Point-estimate check for Log Price model plot( density(ba.log_price$fitted.values), xlim = c(1.5, 8.5), ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05), col = "black", lwd = 2, xlab = "log(1 + Price USD)", ylab = "Density", main = "Point Check: Log Price Model" ) lines(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2) legend("topright", legend = c("Predicted (Fitted)", "Actual"), col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 2.1: Point-Estimate Predictive Checks: Fitted vs. Actual Density for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right).](index_files/figure-html/fig_ppc_point-1.png){width=1056} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) ``` ::: Now we define the `generate_draw()` simulation function to incorporate both **inferential uncertainty** (uncertainty in $\hat{\beta}$) and **predictive uncertainty** (the error variance $\hat{\sigma}^2$), generating $n = 250$ simulated realisations for each model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} generate_draw <- function(m) { # Set up predictors matrix x <- model.matrix(m) # Obtain draws of parameters (inferential uncertainty) sim_bs <- sim(m, 1) # Predicted value mu <- x %*% sim_bs@coef[1, ] # Draw realization incorporating residual sigma (predictive uncertainty) n <- length(mu) y_hat <- rnorm(n, mu, sim_bs@sigma[1]) return(y_hat) } par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1)) # Left panel: Simulated PPC for Raw Price model plot( density(ba.price$fitted.values), xlim = c(-300, 700), ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$price_usd)$y)) * 1.05), col = "white", xlab = "Price (USD)", ylab = "Density", main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Raw Price" ) for (i in 1:250) { tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.price) lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2) } lines(density(ba.price$fitted.values), col = "black", lwd = 2) lines(density(mad_abb$price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2) abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "blue") legend( "topright", legend = c("Actual", "Predicted", "Simulated (n=250)", "Zero Boundary"), col = c("red", "black", "grey60", "blue"), lwd = c(2, 2, 1, 1), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.85 ) # Right panel: Simulated PPC for Log Price model plot( density(ba.log_price$fitted.values), xlim = c(1.5, 8.5), ylim = c(0, max(max(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values)$y), max(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd)$y)) * 1.05), col = "white", xlab = "log(1 + Price USD)", ylab = "Density", main = "Predictive Check (n=250): Log Price" ) for (i in 1:250) { tmp_y <- generate_draw(ba.log_price) lines(density(tmp_y), col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2) } lines(density(ba.log_price$fitted.values), col = "black", lwd = 2) lines(density(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd), col = "red", lwd = 2) legend( "topright", legend = c("Actual", "Predicted", "Simulated (n=250)"), col = c("red", "black", "grey60"), lwd = c(2, 2, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.85 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 2.2: Full Predictive Check with 250 Simulated Realisations (Grey) for the Raw Price Model (left) and Log-Price Model (right).](index_files/figure-html/fig_ppc_sim-1.png){width=1056} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) ``` ::: **Discussion and Model Selection:** 1. **Explanatory Power ($R^2$) and Coefficient Interpretation**: - In both models, `accommodates`, `bathrooms`, and `bedrooms` have statistically significant positive effects on price ($p < 0.001$), whereas `beds` has a statistically significant negative coefficient holding the other predictors constant. This negative partial effect of `beds` arises because, for a fixed number of bedrooms and guests (`bedrooms` and `accommodates` held constant), adding more beds indicates shared/crowded sleeping arrangements (e.g., hostels or subdivided rooms), which command lower nightly rates. - However, the **raw price model (`ba.price`)** explains only **2.3%** of the variance in price ($R^2 = 0.0228$), with a massive residual standard error of **\$358.89**. - By contrast, the **log-price model (`ba.log_price`)** more than doubles the explained variance to **24.4%** ($R^2 = 0.244$). Its coefficients have a clean multiplicative (semi-elasticity) interpretation: each additional guest accommodated increases price by approximately **22%**, an additional bathroom increases price by **-4.4%**, an additional bedroom adds **12.3%**, and an extra bed (holding capacity and bedrooms constant) reduces price by **6.1%**. 2. **Predictive Check Comparison (Why the Log-Price Model is Preferred)**: - **Failure of the Raw Price Model**: Because `price_usd` has extreme positive outliers, the Gaussian error assumption $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ inflates $\hat{\sigma}$ to \$358.9. Consequently, the 250 simulated draws (Figure 2.2, left) form a flat, wide normal curve that completely misses the sharp empirical peak around \$50–\$80 and assigns substantial probability mass to **impossible negative prices** (left of the dashed blue line at \$0). - **Superiority of the Log-Price Model**: In the log-price specification (Figure 2.2, right), while the deterministic point estimates (black curve) are naturally narrower than the observed data (since $\text{Var}(\hat{y}) < \text{Var}(y)$), the 250 simulated draws (grey band) closely envelope the actual empirical distribution (red curve) in location, spread, and symmetry. Furthermore, exponentiating log-price predictions ($\hat{P}_i = \exp(\widehat{\log P_i}) - 1$) guarantees strictly positive price predictions. Therefore, the **log-price model (`ba.log_price`) is strongly preferred**. --- ## Spatial Econometrics: Heterogeneity & Dependence (Chapter 6 Tasks) While the log-price model improves functional form, it treats observations as spatially independent and homogeneous across Madrid. In Chapter 6, we incorporate **spatial heterogeneity** (via neighbourhood fixed effects and spatial regimes) and **spatial dependence** (via spatial weight matrices and exogenous spatial lags) [@anselin1988spatial; @anselin2003spatial; @reyABwolf]. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_map_price <- mad_abb %>% ggplot(aes(color = log1p_price_usd)) + geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75) + scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = "log(1+Price)") + labs(title = "Spatial Distribution of Log AirBnb Prices") + theme_void() + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold")) p_map_nei <- mad_abb %>% ggplot(aes(color = neighbourhood)) + geom_sf(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) + labs(title = paste0("Madrid Neighbourhoods (n = ", length(unique(mad_abb$neighbourhood)), ")")) + theme_void() + theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold")) grid.arrange(p_map_price, p_map_nei, ncol = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 3.1: Spatial Distribution of Log Prices (left) and Neighbourhood Administrative Groupings (right) across Madrid.](index_files/figure-html/fig_price_and_neighbourhood_map-1.png){width=1056} ::: ::: ### Task 6.1: Baseline Non-Spatial Log-Price Model (`m1`) We begin with the baseline non-spatial model explaining `log1p_price_usd` solely through structural property attributes: $$ \log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lm(log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds, data = mad_abb) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -3.8386 -0.4740 -0.1069 0.3130 5.4065 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 3.478207 0.014270 243.751 < 2e-16 *** accommodates 0.219752 0.004641 47.348 < 2e-16 *** bathrooms -0.044322 0.009876 -4.488 7.24e-06 *** bedrooms 0.122788 0.010077 12.184 < 2e-16 *** beds -0.060647 0.005797 -10.462 < 2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 0.7767 on 18394 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.244, Adjusted R-squared: 0.2438 F-statistic: 1484 on 4 and 18394 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: **Interpretation (`m1`):** All four structural predictors are highly statistically significant ($p < 0.001$), explaining **24.4%** of log-price variation. However, `m1` assumes a single global intercept ($\hat{\alpha} = 3.478$) across all of Madrid, ignoring unobserved neighbourhood prestige, accessibility, and locational amenities, which become absorbed into the error term $\epsilon_i$. ### Task 6.2: Spatial Fixed Effects at the Neighbourhood Level (`m2`) To account for **spatial heterogeneity** at the neighbourhood scale, we allow the intercept $\alpha_r$ to vary across each neighbourhood $r \in \{1, \dots, 128\}$ by introducing neighbourhood indicator variables without a global constant (`- 1`): $$ \log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \epsilon_i $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m2 <- lm( log1p_price_usd ~ neighbourhood + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds - 1, data = mad_abb ) # Display the structural property coefficients from the Spatial FE model round(tail(summary(m2)$coefficients, 4), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) accommodates 0.2120 0.0046 46.4276 0 bathrooms -0.0781 0.0096 -8.1311 0 bedrooms 0.1315 0.0098 13.3707 0 beds -0.0592 0.0056 -10.5978 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Spatial FE R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$r.squared, 4), "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m2)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Spatial FE R-squared: 0.9701 | Adjusted R-squared: 0.9698 ``` ::: ::: We now extract the estimated neighbourhood fixed effects ($\hat{\alpha}_r$) and map them to visualise Madrid's **"Geography of Desirability"**. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Extract neighbourhood fixed-effect coefficients coef_df <- data.frame( term = names(m2$coefficients), coef = as.numeric(m2$coefficients), stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) %>% dplyr::filter(str_starts(term, "neighbourhood")) %>% mutate(nei = str_replace(term, "^neighbourhood", "")) # Join fixed effects back to spatial points nei.fes <- coef_df %>% right_join(mad_abb, by = c("nei" = "neighbourhood")) %>% st_as_sf() # Plot the geography of desirability ggplot(nei.fes, aes(color = coef)) + geom_sf(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.85) + scale_color_viridis_c(option = "viridis", name = expression(hat(alpha)[r])) + labs( title = "Geography of Desirability: Neighbourhood Fixed Effects in Madrid", subtitle = "Baseline log-price premium by neighbourhood controlling for property size" ) + theme_void() + theme( plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 3.2: Geography of Desirability in Madrid: Estimated Neighbourhood Fixed Effects (alpha_r) from Model m2.](index_files/figure-html/fig_spatial_fe_map-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: **Interpretation (`m2`):** Introducing neighbourhood fixed effects isolates *within-neighbourhood* variation, controlling for unobserved time-invariant spatial confounders (such as historic architecture, metro access, and prestige). The structural coefficients remain highly significant (`accommodates` = 0.212, `bathrooms` = -0.078, `bedrooms` = 0.132, `beds` = -0.059), and the mapped $\hat{\alpha}_r$ estimates (Figure 3.2) reveal a clear core-periphery and north-south gradient: central and wealthy northern neighbourhoods (*Recoletos*, *Castellana*, *Jerónimos*, *Sol*, *Goya*) command the highest baseline willingness-to-pay, whereas southern working-class neighbourhoods (*San Cristóbal*, *Amposta*, *Entrevías*, *Zofío*) have the lowest baseline intercepts. ### Task 6.3: Spatial Regimes at the Neighbourhood Level (`m3`) Spatial fixed effects (`m2`) allow only the intercept ($\alpha_r$) to vary geographically while restricting the slope parameters ($\beta_1, \dots, \beta_4$) to be uniform across Madrid. **Spatial regimes (`m3`)** generalise spatial heterogeneity by allowing both the intercept and all structural slope coefficients to vary across neighbourhoods: $$ \log(P_i) = \alpha_r + \beta_{r1} Acc_i + \beta_{r2} Bath_i + \beta_{r3} Bedr_i + \beta_{r4} Beds_i + \epsilon_{ri} $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mad_abb$one <- 1 m3 <- lm( log1p_price_usd ~ 0 + (one + accommodates + bathrooms + bedrooms + beds):(neighbourhood), data = mad_abb ) cat("Spatial Regimes R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$r.squared, 4), "| Adjusted R-squared:", round(summary(m3)$adj.r.squared, 4), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Spatial Regimes R-squared: 0.9722 | Adjusted R-squared: 0.9712 ``` ::: ::: Let us compare the nested progression from `m1` (Pooled OLS) to `m2` (Spatial Fixed Effects) to `m3` (Spatial Regimes) using an $F$-test (`anova`) and visualise the distribution of neighbourhood-specific slope estimates $\hat{\beta}_{rk}$ across Madrid. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m1, m2, m3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sr_coefs <- tibble( term = names(coef(m3)), estimate = as.numeric(coef(m3)) ) %>% dplyr::filter(!is.na(estimate)) %>% mutate( variable = case_when( str_starts(term, "accommodates:") ~ "accommodates", str_starts(term, "bathrooms:") ~ "bathrooms", str_starts(term, "bedrooms:") ~ "bedrooms", str_starts(term, "beds:") ~ "beds", TRUE ~ "intercept" ) ) %>% dplyr::filter(variable != "intercept", abs(estimate) < 1.5) global_refs <- tibble( variable = c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds"), global_est = as.numeric(coef(m1)[c("accommodates", "bathrooms", "bedrooms", "beds")]) ) ggplot(sr_coefs, aes(x = estimate)) + geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.85) + geom_vline(data = global_refs, aes(xintercept = global_est), colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) + facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", nrow = 1) + labs( title = "Spatial Regimes (m3): Distribution of Local Slope Coefficients across Neighbourhoods", subtitle = "Red dashed line indicates the global baseline OLS estimate (m1)", x = "Estimated Coefficient (within Neighbourhood)", y = "Number of Neighbourhoods" ) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Figure 3.3: Distribution of Neighbourhood-Specific Slope Estimates (Spatial Regimes Model m3) vs. Global Pooled OLS Estimates (Dashed Red Line).](index_files/figure-html/fig_spatial_regimes_slopes-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: **Interpretation (`m3`):** Allowing slopes to vary by neighbourhood significantly reduces the residual sum of squares compared to both `m1` and `m2` ($p < 0.001$ in the `anova` $F$-test), raising the unadjusted $R^2$ from **0.244** (`m1`) to **0.972** (`m3`). This indicates that the marginal valuation of an extra bedroom or bathroom differs across sub-markets (e.g., central tourist apartments vs. suburban family homes). However, estimating 5 parameters across 128 neighbourhoods consumes over 600 degrees of freedom, causing some small neighbourhoods with few listings to exhibit noisy or unidentifiable (`NA`) slope estimates—a classic bias-variance trade-off in unrestricted spatial regime models. ### Task 6.4: Spatial Weights Matrix & Exogenous Spatial Lag Model (`m4` & `m5`) Unlike spatial heterogeneity (which links outcomes to administrative areas), **spatial dependence** captures how observations interact directly across distance [@anselin2014modern; @gibbons2014spatial]. We construct a row-standardised $k$-nearest neighbours ($k = 50$) spatial weights matrix $W$, where $w_{ij} = 1/50$ if listing $j$ is among the 50 closest properties to listing $i$, and $w_{ij} = 0$ otherwise. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Construct k = 50 nearest-neighbour spatial weights matrix hnn <- mad_abb %>% st_coordinates() %>% as.matrix() %>% knearneigh(k = 50) hnb <- knn2nb(hnn) hknn <- nb2listw(hnb, style = "W") hknn ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Characteristics of weights list object: Neighbour list object: Number of regions: 18399 Number of nonzero links: 919950 Percentage nonzero weights: 0.2717539 Average number of links: 50 Non-symmetric neighbours list Weights style: W Weights constants summary: n nn S0 S1 S2 W 18399 338523201 18399 679.7592 74417.63 ``` ::: ::: First, we verify the presence of global spatial autocorrelation in `log1p_price_usd` and in the baseline OLS residuals (`m1`) using Moran's $I$. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} moran_price <- moran.test(mad_abb$log1p_price_usd, hknn) moran_res <- lm.morantest(m1, hknn) cat("Moran's I on log1p_price_usd:", round(moran_price$estimate[1], 4), "(p-value:", format.pval(moran_price$p.value), ")\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Moran's I on log1p_price_usd: 0.1085 (p-value: < 2.22e-16 ) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat("Moran's I on Baseline m1 Residuals:", round(moran_res$estimate[1], 4), "(p-value:", format.pval(moran_res$p.value), ")\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Moran's I on Baseline m1 Residuals: 0.0995 (p-value: < 2.22e-16 ) ``` ::: ::: **Motivation for the Spatial Lag Variable(s):** We motivate two complementary **Exogenous Spatial Lag (SLX)** models: 1. **Spatial Lag of Bathrooms (`w_bathrooms`, Model `m4`)**: Following the course framework in Chapter 6, the number of bathrooms in a property serves as a proxy for housing size, build quality, and luxury status. The spatial lag $W \cdot \text{Bath}_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \text{Bath}_j$ measures the average number of bathrooms among the 50 nearest surrounding AirBnb listings. If a property is surrounded by large, high-end apartments, positive neighbourhood status externalities and local market comparables should raise its nightly price even holding its own structural characteristics constant: $$ \log(P_i) = \alpha + \beta_1 Acc_i + \beta_2 Bath_i + \beta_3 Bedr_i + \beta_4 Beds_i + \beta_5 Bath_{\text{lag}-i} + \epsilon_i $$ 2. **Spatial Lag of Guest Capacity (`w_accommodates`) & Distance to El Retiro (`km_to_retiro`, Model `m5`)**: In Madrid, proximity to the city's premier green/cultural landmark (`km_to_retiro`) and the surrounding density of large tourist accommodations (`w_accommodates`) alongside `w_bathrooms` capture both local housing prestige and urban centrality externalities. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Compute spatial lags using W (k = 50 nearest neighbours) mad_abb$w_bathrooms <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$bathrooms) mad_abb$w_accommodates <- lag.listw(hknn, mad_abb$accommodates) # Model m4: Baseline + Spatial lag of bathrooms (w_bathrooms) m4 <- lm( log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bedrooms + beds + bathrooms + w_bathrooms, data = mad_abb ) summary(m4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = log1p_price_usd ~ accommodates + bedrooms + beds + bathrooms + w_bathrooms, data = mad_abb) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -3.9168 -0.4665 -0.1036 0.3065 5.4483 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Econometrically, this demonstrates strong **exogenous spatial spillovers**: while a single apartment's bathroom count is noisy, the average bathroom count of the 50 surrounding listings acts as a robust local indicator of housing stock wealth and neighbourhood prestige. In `m5`, adding `w_accommodates` (0.091, $p < 0.001$) and distance to El Retiro Park (`km_to_retiro` = 0.0156, $p < 0.001$, indicating an approximate 1.6% price decay per kilometre away from El Retiro) further improves model fit (Adjusted $R^2 = 0.2512$, AIC = 4.27438\times 10^{4}), confirming that both local spatial context and urban centrality are critical determinants of AirBnb prices in Madrid. --- ## References
